name: Brooks's Law
statement: Adding manpower to a late software project makes it later.
meaning: Throwing more people at a project that is already behind usually pushes the finish line further out, not closer.
mechanism: New people are not instantly productive: someone already on the project has to stop working to train them, and every extra person multiplies the communication channels that must be kept in sync. For a while the ramp-up cost and the coordination overhead outweigh the added labour, so the schedule slips further before it improves — if it improves at all.
example: A release is a month late, so management adds five engineers in week one. The existing team spends the next fortnight onboarding them and untangling who owns what; velocity drops before it recovers, and the date slips again.
whyItMatters: It punctures the intuition that people and time are interchangeable — that a job needing twelve person-months can be done by twelve people in one. A late project is more often rescued by cutting scope or holding the team steady than by staffing up in a panic.
misreadings: It does not say adding people never helps — early, before the crunch, more hands can genuinely speed things up. The claim is narrow: adding people to an already-late project, mid-flight, tends to backfire because the onboarding and coordination costs land exactly when there is no slack to absorb them.
origin: Coined by the software engineer Fred Brooks in his 1975 book The Mythical Man-Month, drawing on his experience managing the development of IBM's OS/360.

sources.text: Brooks, F. P. (1975). The Mythical Man-Month: Essays on Software Engineering. Addison-Wesley.
